meta.title: Who really said "My Mind Is Made Up. Don’t Confuse Me With the Facts"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Nobody named. Roy S. Durstine printed the kernel in 1945, quoting an unnamed client; the two-part joke spread anonymously on office signs by 1954.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'My Mind Is Made Up. Don't Confuse Me With the Facts'?
meta.ogDescription: An anonymous office joke. Durstine’s 1945 article has the kernel — from a client he never named — and the full saying is on signs by 1954.

answer.label: Not Roy S. Durstine’s own line — an anonymous office joke
answer.authorName: Unknown — anonymous; first root printed by Roy S. Durstine
answer.authorDates: Kernel in print November 1945 · full two-part saying circulating by March 1954
answer.sourceLine: The earliest relevant evidence Quote Investigator has found ↗ is a November 1945 article in Advertising & Selling titled “Don’t Confuse Me With Facts!” by the advertising man Roy S. Durstine. But Durstine was not the speaker: he was recounting a meeting in which a client, having heard a survey demolish his strategy, reached for a cigarette and said softly, “Don’t confuse me with facts!” Durstine never named him. The familiar two-part version — with “My mind is made up” attached — turns up only in 1954, on signs and pocket cards, with no author claimed.

source.excerpt: The client stared at the presentation, deep in thought. At last he reached for a cigarette and said softly: “Don’t confuse me with facts!”
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ names the 1945 Durstine article in Advertising & Selling (p. 34, verified on paper) as the earliest pertinent evidence, crediting Professor Jonathan Lighter with locating it.

QI states its conclusion as a hypothesis, not a finding: the saying “can be traced back to” Durstine’s article, in which “My mind is made up” was only implicit in the context — and Durstine “did not precisely identify the person who said” the line.

The compound saying is documented on signs and cards through 1954: a Democrat’s desk sign in the Daily Sitka Sentinel (10 March), Fred Gymer’s mottoes in the Chicago Tribune (23 May), Bennett Cerf’s “Trade Winds” in The Saturday Review (3 July) and pocket cards reported by The New York Times (5 July). None carries an attribution.

The wording on this page matches Cerf’s July 1954 report exactly — “Sign in an editor’s office: ‘My mind is made up. Don’t confuse me with the facts.’” — which is the earliest appearance of this phrasing that QI documents ↗.
source.excerptNote: Durstine’s own anecdote, as transcribed by Quote Investigator ↗. Note what is missing: the words “My mind is made up,” and any name for the man who spoke.

source.rightsNote: No rights status can honestly be asserted. The saying itself is anonymous — no author has ever been identified for the two-part wording — so there is no rights holder to name. Separately, every printed appearance documented so far (1945, 1954) postdates 1931, so none of those articles is in the public domain in the United States either. quotle.info makes no public-domain claim here.

author.name: Roy S. Durstine
author.heading: About Roy S. Durstine
author.metaLine: 1886–1962 · American reporter, author & advertising executive — co-founder of BBDO
author.bio: Roy S. Durstine was one of the founders of the advertising agency that became Batten, Barton, Durstine & Osborn, and a prolific writer about the trade. By 1939 he had left to run his own shop, Roy S. Durstine, Inc. — the byline under which the 1945 article appeared. That piece is the earliest known appearance of this saying’s kernel, but he was quoting a client, not himself, and he pointedly did not give the man’s name.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: Quotation sites file this under Durstine because his is the only name attached to the earliest citation. That is a filing convention, not an attribution.

items.why: He wrote the 1945 article, but the line in it belongs to a client he deliberately left unnamed, and his version omits “My mind is made up” — QI ↗.

items.who: Fred Gymer, Bennett Cerf, Ed Place
items.why: All three are recorded circulating the saying in 1954 — as a motto, a magazine filler and a pocket card respectively — and none of them claimed it, per QI’s citations ↗.

items.who: Sen. George D. Aiken (1954) and Rep. Earl Landgrebe (1974)
items.why: Aiken used it to amuse a closed committee in August 1954, while the saying was still spreading on office signs and pocket cards; Landgrebe said “Don’t confuse me with facts: I’ve got a closed mind” in 1974 while opposing Nixon’s impeachment. Neither coined it — QI ↗.
QI ↗ records a 2002 philosophy primer linking a version of the line to Plato, while conceding he “was probably not the first to say” it. There is no ancient source.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest answer is that an unnamed advertising client said something close to it in or before 1945, and an anonymous sign-maker finished the joke by 1954. QI’s trail ↗ is the best account anyone has.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The joke had a first life as shop-talk about advertising. Durstine’s article is not a complaint about the client — it is a defence of him: advertising is more art than science, Durstine argued, and a proprietor with a record of being right should not be overruled by a survey. The line only became a weapon later, once it was detached from that argument and printed on a card you could flash at people.

By 1954 it was office furniture — a desk sign, a monthly motto letter, a vest-pocket card for deflecting a bore in Washington. That is the life cycle of a good aphorism with no owner: everybody repeats it, nobody signs it.
detailsBody: The 1974 use is the one most people half-remember. Earl Landgrebe ↗, an Indiana Republican holding out against Nixon’s impeachment in the president’s final week, told reporters “Don’t confuse me with facts: I’ve got a closed mind.” QI cites the Wall Street Journal of 9 October 1974 for it ↗. It reads today as an admission. At the time it was a man reaching for a familiar office gag and badly misjudging the room.
context.pull: Durstine wrote it down to defend the client. It survives as a way of mocking him.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator gives the earliest pertinent evidence as a November 1945 article 'Don't Confuse Me With Facts!' by Roy S. Durstine in Advertising & Selling, quote page 34.

In Durstine's anecdote the line is spoken by an unnamed client, and QI states Durstine 'did not precisely identify the person who said' it; QI also notes 'My mind is made up' was only implicit in the context.

QI documents the full saying on signs and cards in 1954 — Daily Sitka Sentinel 10 March, Chicago Tribune 23 May (Fred Gymer), Saturday Review 3 July (Bennett Cerf), New York Times 5 July, Washington Post 12 August (Ed Place) — and Bennett Cerf's July 1954 version reads 'My mind is made up. Don't confuse me with the facts.'
Roy Sarles Durstine (13 December 1886 – 28 November 1962) was an American advertising executive who co-founded BBDO and from 1939 was president of Roy S. Durstine, Inc.

QI records Sen. George D. Aiken using the saying in an August 1954 committee hearing, Rep. Earl Landgrebe saying 'Don't confuse me with facts: I've got a closed mind' in 1974, and a 2002 book linking a version to Plato.
